summary: This informational document proposes the "altc" attribute for SDP, which lets one offer carry multiple IP addresses of different address families, such as IPv4 and IPv6. It avoids the backward-compatibility problems of ANAT. It is meant for cases where connectivity checks are not needed; where they are, ICE applies.

eli5.summary: This lets one call invitation list both old-style and new-style addresses, so the other side can use whichever works.

questions: offering ipv4 and ipv6 addresses in one sdp
how to offer ipv4 and ipv6 in one sdp
subtitle: Let a video call offer both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses in one message.

tldr.problem: When two programs want to set up a video or audio call, they must agree on which IP version (IPv4 or IPv6) to use. If one program only knows about IPv4 and the other only about IPv6, they cannot talk to each other.
tldr.mechanism: The ALTC (Alternate Connectivity) attribute lets a call invitation list multiple addresses of different types in one message. The other side picks the one that works for it.
tldr.outcome: A dual-stack program can now talk to IPv4-only or IPv6-only programs without needing special relay hardware in between. This is simpler and faster than the older ANAT approach.

facts.label: Backward compatibility
facts.value: Yes; legacy systems safely ignore altc attributes

today: RFC 6947 is an Informational RFC that has not been obsoleted. ALTC has been implemented in SIP systems and used in production networks for IPv6 transition. It remains a simple, lightweight alternative to more complex mechanisms like ICE for scenarios where connectivity checks are not needed and both sides trust the connection information they exchange.

sections.title: The IPv4 and IPv6 Problem
sections.content:
The Internet is moving from IPv4 addresses (like 192.0.2.1) to IPv6 addresses (like 2001:db8::1), but the two versions cannot talk to each other directly. Many devices today support both, called dual-stack, but others still support only one. When a program that supports both tries to set up a video call with another program, it needs a way to offer both kinds of addresses so the other side can choose whichever works.

The old approach, called ANAT, tried to do this but caused problems: older call systems would reject the invitation as broken because they did not understand the extra information. So ALTC was created as a backward-compatible replacement, using an attribute format that legacy systems simply ignore.
sections.eli5: Imagine you are moving to a new house but still want to get phone calls. You can give people both your old phone number and your new one, and they will reach you on whichever one works.

sections.title: How ALTC Works
sections.content:
The ALTC mechanism uses the Session Description Protocol (SDP), which is the language programs use to describe call setup. Each media stream (like audio or video) in the invitation normally lists one IP address in the connection line. ALTC adds extra lines, called altc attributes, that list alternative addresses and ports.

The sender lists its most likely address in the main connection line for backward compatibility, then uses altc lines to list alternatives. It also includes a duplicate altc line with the primary address, so the receiver can detect if a middlebox changed the address. The receiver picks an address from the list that works for it, and answers with that address in its response.
sections.eli5: The invitation says 'I am probably at 192.0.2.1, but you might reach me better at 2001:db8::1.' The other person picks one and calls back there.

sections.title: The Syntax and Rules
sections.content:
An altc attribute has the form a=altc:1 IP6 2001:db8::1 45678, where the number indicates preference order (1 is best), IP6 or IP4 is the address type, the next field is the actual address, and the last is the port number. Each media stream with altc MUST include at least two altc lines: one for the primary address and port (a duplicate of what is already in the invitation), and one for the alternative.

Only one altc attribute per address type is allowed in each media stream, so the receiver can tell from the address family in the answer which alternative was accepted. The mechanism does not support offering different protocols (like TCP versus UDP) or codecs; it only varies the address and port.
sections.eli5: You list your addresses in order of preference, with the phone number and type of service that works best first.

sections.title: Behavior in Mixed Networks
sections.content:
ALTC works well in managed networks where the system running the call software controls both the sending and receiving sides, or where they can be trusted to understand ALTC. If an old-style middlebox in the network changed the connection address but did not understand ALTC, the receiver would notice the mismatch between the altered address in the c= line and what the altc attributes claim, and would ignore altc and use the altered address instead. This ensures the call goes through even if the middlebox broke the ALTC information.

When both sides support ICE, a more sophisticated connection negotiation protocol, either ICE or ALTC can be used but not both. ALTC is lighter-weight and works in simpler cases; ICE adds more capabilities but requires more computation. ALTC can also be combined with other SDP features like RTP multiplexing or capability negotiation without conflict.
sections.eli5: If something breaks the invitation, you still fall back to the main address so the call does not fail. If you have fancier tools like ICE, you use one or the other, not both.

sections.title: Real-World Scenarios
sections.content:
ALTC is designed for service providers deploying IPv6 to their customers while their core network still runs IPv4. A Signaling Border Element (an edge router for call setup) can accept a call from an IPv6 client, create both an IPv6-to-IPv6 and IPv6-to-IPv4 relay path, and send an invitation listing both addresses. The receiving side picks the one that works, and if both support IPv6, the call goes directly IPv6 to IPv6 without any relay in between.

Another use case involves programs behind Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN) devices, which are networks where multiple customers share one public IPv4 address. If the software has both IPv4 and IPv6 interfaces, ALTC lets it offer both in the invitation, allowing calls to avoid the CGN when IPv6 is available and reducing the load on NAT hardware.
sections.eli5: A phone company can offer both old phone numbers and new ones and let the customer pick which works best.
